chief_complaint: sudden brief spinning vertigo lasting 20 seconds triggered when rolling over in bed or looking up at shelves (BPPV)
hpi_details: 66F presents with 3-week history of sudden, intense spinning dizzy spells that last exactly 15 to 30 seconds per episode. Vertigo is triggered reliably by specific head movements: turning over in bed to the right, lying flat in bed at night, or tilting her head straight upward to reach the top kitchen shelf. During the brief 20-second spin, feels intensely nauseated, but as soon as she holds her head perfectly still, the spinning completely stops within half a minute. Zero hearing loss, ringing in ears, or headache.
ideas: thinks she has a blocked neck artery or early brain stroke causing dizzy attacks when turning head
concerns: terrified of falling down or losing balance while walking
expectations: wants brain MRI and physical therapy to stop the room from spinning every time she lies down

clinical_knowledge.topic: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes bedside canalith repositioning (Epley maneuver) with reassurance against unnecessary imaging or medication, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden brief spinning vertigo lasting 20 seconds triggered when rolling over in bed or looking up at shelves (BPPV)

Key HPI features: 66F presents with 3-week history of sudden, intense spinning dizzy spells that last exactly 15 to 30 seconds per episode. Vertigo is triggered reliably by specific head movements: turning over in bed to the right, lying flat in bed at night, or tilting her head straight upward to reach the top kitchen shelf. During the brief 20-second spin, feels intensely nauseated, but as soon as she holds her head perfectly still, the spinning completely stops within half a minute. Zero hearing loss, ringing in ears, or headache.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 72, BP 130/80. Otoscopic and neurological exams completely normal. Diagnostic Dix-Hallpike Provocation Maneuver (rapidly lowering patient from sitting to supine with head turned 45 degrees to the right and extended 20 degrees over bed edge): after a latency of 3-5 seconds, patient experiences severe subjective spinning vertigo accompanied by classic torsional, upbeating geotropic nystagmus (beating toward the dependent right ear). Nystagmus peaks and fatigues/ceases completely within 25 seconds. Sitting back up triggers mild reversal nystagmus. Testing the left ear is negative. Findings definitively confirm Canalithiasis of the Right Posterior Semicircular Canal (free-floating calcium carbonate otolith debris otoconia trapped inside the posterior canal).
Current medications: Alendronate weekly, Amlodipine 5mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vestibular neuritis (constant, not positional) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any hearing loss or persistent symptoms between episodes — would suggest a diagnosis other than BPPV.
management_principles: Perform immediate bedside therapeutic Canalith Repositioning Procedure (Epley Maneuver) for the right posterior canal: systematically rotating the head through 4 sequential 90-degree steps (holding each position for 30-60 seconds until nystagmus clears) to float the trapped otoconia debris out of the semicircular canal back into the vestibule/utricle where it is harmlessly absorbed
Epley maneuver achieves >85% curative success in a single 5-minute session
Reassure patient that brain MRI and daily vestibular suppressant drugs (meclizine) are unnecessary and unhelpful for free-floating otolith repositioning
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 66F presenting with short-duration (<1 minute) episodic positional vertigo triggered specifically by changes in head position relative to gravity, classic for Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

Diagnostic Dix-Hallpike Provocation Maneuver (rapidly lowering patient from sitting to supine with head turned 45 degrees to the right and extended 20 degrees over bed edge): after a latency of 3-5 seconds, patient experiences severe subjective spinning vertigo accompanied by classic torsional, upbeating geotropic nystagmus (beating toward the dependent right ear). reference_soap.assessment: Right Posterior Semicircular Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV - Canalithiasis).

Perform immediate bedside therapeutic Canalith Repositioning Procedure (Epley Maneuver) for the right posterior canal: systematically rotating the head through 4 sequential 90-degree steps (holding each position for 30-60 seconds until nystagmus clears) to float the trapped otoconia debris out of the semicircular canal back into the vestibule/utricle where it is harmlessly absorbed. Epley maneuver achieves >85% curative success in a single 5-minute session. 2. Reassure patient that brain MRI and daily vestibular suppressant drugs (meclizine) are unnecessary and unhelpful for free-floating otolith repositioning.

learning_objectives: Perform and interpret the diagnostic Dix-Hallpike maneuver (identifying latency, duration <1 minute, fatigability, and upbeating torsional nystagmus beating toward the affected dependent ear confirming Posterior Canal BPPV)
Explain the pathophysiology of Canalithiasis (calcium carbonate otoconia crystals dislodged from the utricle macula floating freely within the semicircular canal endolymph)
Execute the step-by-step therapeutic Epley Canalith Repositioning Maneuver to definitively cure posterior canal BPPV at the bedside

Differentiate peripheral positional nystagmus (latent onset, fatigable, torsional/upbeating, suppressed by visual fixation) from central brainstem/cerebellar nystagmus (pure vertical/downbeating, immediate onset, non-fatiguing, no latency, accompanied by neurological deficits)

teaching.one_liner: Dislodged calcium crystals in the inner ear canal cause brief, intense spinning triggered by specific head movements (rolling over, looking up), lasting under a minute — cured in most cases by a single Epley maneuver, no MRI needed.
red_flags: Any hearing loss or persistent symptoms between episodes — would suggest a diagnosis other than BPPV

must_ask.say: Does the spinning happen specifically when you roll over in bed or look up?
Does each spinning spell last less than a minute?
Any ringing in your ears or hearing changes?
How many weeks has this been happening?
Are you worried about falling during these episodes?
